PullRequest.Title: chat: prioritize paste choices over the agent picker shortcut
PullRequest.Body:
<!-- Thank you for submitting a Pull Request. Please:

Let Ctrl/Cmd+Period open active paste/drop choices in the workbench chat input instead of the agent picker, while preserving the normal picker shortcut.

Fixes #322164.

<!--
Validation:
- `pnpm run build-fast` - passed full client, extension, extension-media, and Copilot build with private lockfile-matched dependencies.
- `pnpm run build-fast --client-only` - passed for the final candidate.
- `./scripts/test.sh --run src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/test/browser/actions/chatExecuteActions.test.ts --run src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/test/browser/accessibility/chatAccessibilityHelp.test.ts --run src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/test/browser/widget/input/editor/chatPasteProviders.test.ts --run src/vs/editor/contrib/dropOrPasteInto/test/browser/copyPasteController.test.ts --reporter dot` - passed, 134 tests.
- `pnpm run typecheck-client` - passed for the final candidate.
- `pnpm run eslint src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/browser/actions/chatExecuteActions.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/browser/actions/chatAccessibilityHelp.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/test/browser/actions/chatExecuteActions.test.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/test/browser/accessibility/chatAccessibilityHelp.test.ts` - passed, four files.
- `git diff --check` - passed.

Before the fix, the new shortcut regression failed on Windows, Linux, and macOS mappings. A separate accessibility-help scope regression was also observed failing before the final guard.

Live macOS validation used an isolated authenticated Copilot workbench, actual TypeScript symbol and paste providers, an in-page clipboard transfer instead of the shared system clipboard, and real keyboard events. Before the fix, Cmd+Period opened Agent/Ask choices after a symbol paste. Afterward, it opened Pasted Symbol Reference / Insert Plain Text; ArrowDown and Enter replaced #sym:PasteExample with PasteExample and removed the symbol attachment. Escape restored input focus and dismissed the widget; the normal agent-picker shortcut then worked again. No chat request was sent.

The full registered runtime keybinding resolver passed 18 cases across Windows Ctrl+Period, Linux Ctrl+Period, and macOS Cmd+Period: normal chat picker, chat paste/drop choices, ordinary editor paste/drop choices, and editor quick fix. Explicit user bindings are covered by the focused unit tests.

Scope and limitations: this fixes the original regular-workbench issue. The separate pre-existing Agents-window untitled-draft picker binding is unchanged; the new help text is scoped accordingly. Native Windows/Linux UI, screen-reader interaction, and live drop gestures were not exercised locally. Final-head hosted CI and Copilot review results are reported separately.
-->

Scenarios.Scenario: Workbench startup loads chat contributions and registers the Open Agent Picker action.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Workbench module evaluation and synchronous action/keybinding registration must complete during startup. The added controller imports do not add a new module-evaluation boundary because workbench.common.main imports editor.all before chat.shared.contribution, and editor.all already imports both paste/drop contributions and their controller modules.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One workbench renderer startup and one OpenModePickerAction registration; cost is constant and does not scale with editors, chats, messages, or providers.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single-threaded, serialized ES module evaluation followed by synchronous registry mutation; no queue, limiter, or asynchronous fan-out is involved.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Each ES module is evaluated once per renderer/module graph. Cold startup already evaluates both controller modules through editor.all; subsequent chat registration reuses the evaluated module bindings. There is no positive, negative, or miss cache introduced by the diff.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the entrypoint import order and editor.all contribution imports directly establish prior loading, while the changed action constructor only builds two additional context expressions.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact module-loader timings vary by build, but the dependency graph proves the changed imports do not add first-time evaluation of these modules on the normal workbench startup path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The suspected eager-loading mechanism is absent on the product startup path, and the added registration work is two constant-size context-key expressions.

Scenarios.Scenario: A user presses Ctrl/Cmd+Period in a normal chat input or while a paste/drop selector is visible.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Synchronous keybinding resolution must inspect the action's when-clause before dispatch. The diff adds two boolean context-key predicates; ContextKeyAndExpr evaluates these as short-circuiting local context lookups. Paste/drop selector handling remains in the existing editor commands and controllers.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One specific Ctrl/Cmd+Period event; added work remains two lookups regardless of document size, attachment count, provider count, or chat history.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One synchronous resolver invocation per key event; there is no asynchronous work, concurrency burst, queue, or backpressure change.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Cold and warm behavior are equivalent for the changed predicates: they read already-maintained context-key values. The diff adds no cache, cache key, invalidation path, negative lookup, or coalescing behavior.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed when-clause and ContextKeyAndExpr.evaluate implementation establish exactly two extra short-circuitable in-memory evaluations, with no controller invocation or boundary call added by resolution.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Hardware-dependent nanosecond-level lookup cost is not measured, but cardinality and code path are certain and bounded to two extra predicates on the relevant key event.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The input-path work is constant, local, allocation-free during evaluation, and does not scale with user data or invoke an expensive boundary.

Scenarios.Scenario: A user opens accessibility help on a supported workbench chat surface.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The help provider synchronously assembles localized strings and joins them before showing the accessible view. The diff adds one constant localized sentence and one array push only on non-inline, non-sessions-window surfaces.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One help invocation; added CPU and allocation are O(1) and independent of chats, messages, attachments, editors, and workspace resources.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single synchronous help-text construction per invocation; no parallelism, serialization queue, or background task is involved.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Help text is generated per provider opening both before and after the diff. The new string has no cache lifecycle or invalidation behavior; localization data is local and no network or filesystem lookup occurs on this path.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the complete changed branch and provider call path show one bounded string addition, with no transitive subprocess, IPC, filesystem, database, or network operation.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The exact added bytes depend on localization, but the addition is one bounded sentence and cannot grow with chat history or workspace size.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The bounded string allocation is negligible relative to the existing one-shot help construction and introduces no scaling or retention mechanism.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all four changed files and traced startup registration, keybinding dispatch, and accessibility-help generation. No diff-introduced hot/scaling work, expensive-boundary fan-out, unbounded retention, cache lifecycle issue, or concrete performance regression was found.
